fix: Give each round an ACL2-decided deadline or work quantum that yields to the next due peer, and drive pull and feed links from the nonblocking mux (or one worker per peer under an ACL2 admission bound). Make dials nonblocking, with completion observed by the loop.
reviewer: pull-service.lisp:448-456 loops until the session is done or stopping. Each receive uses a 60 s read timeout (line 40), and nothing bounds the round's wall time: a grep of books/peer-pull-session.lisp finds no deadline, budget or clock. A peer that sends one byte every 59 s therefore holds the round indefinitely. fnn-pull-worker (lines 521-546) runs every due peer's round and then fnn-catchup-tick sequentially on one thread, so all other pull and catch-up work waits. On the push side, fnn-feed-dial (feed-service.lisp:418) calls fnn-peer-connect with a blocking timeout inside the sole worker loop (lines 549-558). DNS is noted as a separate unbounded boundary (lines 402-403). Each dial retry stalls the pump of every established link for that long. Pull peers are operator-configured, which limits who can do this.
scenario: A configured pull peer, or anything on the path to it, sends one byte every 59 s. Each receive succeeds, so the round never ends: no wall-clock or work budget bounds a round (books/peer-pull-session.lisp has none). Every other pull peer and every catch-up round wait indefinitely. For the push feed, one peer whose DNS or TCP connect hangs for the ACL2 timeout blocks the pump of every other established link for that long, on every backoff retry. This is the disconnected-operation path, where slow and lossy peers are expected.
title: Pull, catch-up and push feeds each run on one serial thread with blocking I/O and no per-round deadline, so one slow peer starves the rest
